query: Single-phase ZrB2 benefits from strong Zr–B and B–B interactions and a high melting point, but it requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and does not readily meet application requirements on its own. Earlier studies sought to lower the required temperature, yet the resulting materials remained vulnerable to high-temperature oxidation or liquid plating-metal corrosion, while reported preparation temperatures generally remained above 1700 °C. Under the constraints of lower-temperature manufacture, adequate strength and structural integrity, oxidation durability, and prolonged service in a liquid plating bath, what single intervention could overcome these limitations? Provide one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome compared with single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens, applicable preparation and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment evaluating final body quality, structural integrity, oxidation, and liquid-metal corrosion that would falsify the hypothesis if its predictions were not observed.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a small, optimized amount of a Si-based additive, such as a controlled SiO2 precursor, into the ZrB2 powder mix during spark plasma sintering at 1600–1700 °C promotes the in situ formation of a borosilicate glass phase along the grain boundaries, thereby enhancing densification, mechanical integrity, high-temperature oxidation resistance, and liquid plating-metal corrosion resistance compared with both conventionally high-temperature (above 2300 °C) single-phase ZrB2 and previously lower-temperature specimens.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase ZrB2 prepared at >2300 °C that relies on strong Zr–B/B–B bonding but shows susceptibility to oxidation and corrosion when processed at lower temperatures.
generation.intervention: Add a controlled amount of a Si-based precursor (e.g., SiO2) into the ZrB2 precursor mixture prior to spark plasma sintering at reduced temperatures (1600–1700 °C).
generation.conditions: Sintering is performed in an inert (argon) atmosphere at 1600–1700 °C; subsequent tests are conducted under high-temperature oxidation environments and in conditions simulating prolonged exposure to liquid plating metals.
generation.structural_mediator: The in situ–formed borosilicate glass phase along ZrB2 grain boundaries that promotes grain bonding and acts as a physical barrier to oxygen diffusion and metal attack.
generation.mechanism: During spark plasma sintering at lower temperatures, the Si-based additive reacts with available boron (and trace oxygen) to form a borosilicate phase that coats the grain boundaries. This intergranular phase improves densification at lower sintering temperatures, reinforces the ceramic microstructure, and inhibits the ingress of oxygen and liquid metals, thereby mitigating oxidation and corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Si-modified ZrB2 is expected to achieve densification and mechanical properties comparable to or better than conventionally sintered ZrB2, while demonstrating significantly improved oxidation resistance and reduced liquid-metal corrosion compared to both high-temperature single-phase ZrB2 and earlier lower-temperature, non-modified specimens.
generation.baseline: High-temperature (>2300 °C) single-phase ZrB2 and lower-temperature (≈1700 °C) processed specimens without Si-based additives, which have exhibited vulnerability to high-temperature oxidation and liquid plating-metal corrosion.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under spark plasma sintering conditions at 1600–1700 °C and service conditions involving high-temperature oxidation (e.g., up to 1100 °C) and exposure to liquid plating metals; deviations in additive concentration or sintering atmosphere might alter outcomes.
generation.uncertainty: Exact optimal concentration of the Si-based additive and the kinetics of borosilicate phase formation require further calibration; process variations and long-term stability of the protective phase under cyclic thermal and corrosive environments are not fully defined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of ceramic samples: (1) conventional high-temperature (>2300 °C) single-phase ZrB2, (2) ZrB2 processed at 1600–1700 °C without any Si additive, and (3) ZrB2 with an optimized SiO2 addition processed at 1600–1700 °C by spark plasma sintering. Characterize each set for densification, microstructure (especially grain boundary phases via TEM/EDS), mechanical strength (via Vickers hardness), oxidation resistance (by isothermal oxidation tests and TGA in flowing dry air), and liquid metal corrosion (through exposure in a simulated plating-metal bath and subsequent weight, microstructure, and phase analysis).
measurements: Density and porosity assessment (using Archimedes method)
Vickers hardness testing at multiple loads
Oxidation weight gain and oxide scale thickness measurements (via TGA and SEM)
Corrosion behavior evaluation (weight change and microscopic characterization after liquid metal exposure)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Si-modified ZrB2 does not show statistically significant improvements (e.g., at least a 20% reduction in oxidation weight gain and corrosion damage while maintaining or improving densification and hardness compared to both controls) under identical conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Hardness and oxidation measurements were conducted using all six single-phase high-entropy diborides (HEB #1-#5 and #7) and six individual metal diboride benchmarking specimens (HfB2, ZrB2, TaB2, NbB2, TiB2, and CrB2) that were made by the same HEBM and SPS fabrication method using the same processing parameters, with one exception that CrB2 was sintered at lower temperature of 1800 °C because its substantially lower melting (and therefore sintering) temperature. MoB2 was not examined because it is not a thermodynamically stable phase (and will decompose to MoB and Mo2B5) below 1500 °C. Hardness measurements were performed with a Vickers’ diamond indenter at 200 kgf/mm2 with a hold time of 15 seconds. The indentations were examined for conformation with the ASTM C1327. The indentations averaged 20–25 μm in width during the testing. Multiple measurements were performed at different locations of each specimen; the mean and standard deviation are reported. Excessive boron powder and Ketjenblack carbon were added to ensure the complete removal of volatilizable oxide impurities (e.g., B2O3) and the in situ synthesis of boron carbide. The HEB/boron carbide composite powders acquired above (fig. S1) were further pressed into pellets, and the rapid liquid-phase high-temperature sintering process was conducted as the treatment temperature was elevated to 3000 K by a carbon-based heater and maintained for 2 min (see details in Materials and Methods). chosen.lever: Si-based dopant addition (e.g., incorporation of a controlled amount of SiC) that promotes in situ formation of a self-healing borosilicate protective layer
chosen.conditions: Processing at 1600–1700 °C under an inert atmosphere, followed by rigorous high-temperature oxidation and liquid-metal corrosion testing in conditions simulating service environments
chosen.why: This single intervention is chosen because it directly addresses the performance limitation of oxidation and liquid-metal corrosion vulnerability. The Si-based dopant not only lowers the sintering temperature through enhanced densification but also triggers a reaction during service that forms a protective borosilicate scale, thereby overcoming the previous issues of high processing temperature and insufficient durability observed in both single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens. The use of spark plasma sintering is well-established in the field for both lowering fabrication temperatures and controlling microstructural properties.

frame.goal: Develop a single-intervention modification that enables lower-temperature manufacture (around or below 1700 °C) while maintaining or enhancing strength, structural integrity, oxidation resistance, and resistance to liquid plating-metal corrosion.
frame.limitation: Single-phase ZrB2 requires extremely high processing temperatures and, when processed at lower temperatures (as in earlier studies), the materials suffer from high-temperature oxidation and liquid plating-metal corrosion issues.
constraints: prolonged service in a liquid plating bath
frame.regime: Operational in high-temperature oxidation environments as well as in contact with liquid plating metals, which impose corrosive and thermally demanding conditions on the material.

decision.trend: Earlier work on high‐temperature diboride ceramics has moved from conventional very high-temperature processing (>2300 °C) toward new processing schemes that lower the sintering temperature. For example, liquid‐precursor methods and spark plasma sintering have been applied to achieve dense, single‐phase high-entropy or multicomponent diboride powders at temperatures around 1800 °C or even near 1700 °C. These routes improved densification and microstructural integrity at lower temperatures compared with traditional approaches. However, despite lowering the required temperature, the materials still lack a built-in means to protect against high-temperature oxidation or liquid plating-metal corrosion.
decision.unsolved: The critical challenge remains: how to design a single-intervention approach that not only enables lower-temperature manufacture (around 1600–1700 °C) but also ensures that the resultant ZrB2 maintains enhanced strength, structural integrity, oxidation durability, and resistance to liquid metal corrosion. Previous approaches have improved densification but left the surfaces vulnerable due to the absence of an in situ formed protective phase.
decision.lever: incorporate a controlled Si‐based additive into the ZrB2 precursor mix
decision.why: Adding a small, optimized amount of a Si-based component (such as a SiO2 precursor that reacts during spark plasma sintering) can promote densification at 1600–1700 °C while also in situ generating a borosilicate phase that adheres to the grain boundaries. This intergranular protective layer will increase oxidation resistance and resist liquid plating metal corrosion, directly addressing the limitations observed in earlier lower-temperature processed specimens. This intervention occupies the niche focused on both chemical modification for process-related densification and for imparting a chemically protective surface, as supported by trends in the related literature.
